Hi again,   I’ve worked with both LiDAR-based and visual SLAM on mobile robots, and from my experience, VSLAM is definitely more tricky to get working reliably compared to LiDAR-based methods.   One of the main challenges is the university labs or indoor test areas often have lots of texture-less areas, which makes keypoint detection unreliable. Another issue is sensor synchronization. For good results, especially with visual-inertial systems, you need a very good synchronized camera and IMU data. For example, if your camera runs at 20 Hz and your IMU at 100 Hz, you need about 5 well-timed IMU samples per frame which is critical for most visual odometry systems.   I haven’t used RTAB-Map on a robot directly, but I’ve tested OpenVINS and ORB-SLAM3 on a real robot. You can see here: https://github.com/M2219/ACNMR and https://github.com/M2219/open_vins.   I found OpenVINS to be better written and more stable than ORB-SLAM3. It doesn’t do full mapping, but it’s lightweight and works well for tracking. This could actually be a good fit for your use case especially on the Jetson Orin Nano, if you combine it with an object detector to locate the specimen.   If you're aiming for dense 3D mapping (not just tracking or detection), things get a bit harder. RTAB-Map can do that, but running it together with post-processing or refinement scripts might face the limits of an 8GB Orin Nano. However, it’s still worth a try, you might get good enough performance with the right tuning.   I personally haven’t tested these on a Nano, since I’ve mostly used a Jetson AGX Orin 40GB and never had memory issues.   In short:   I didn’t get great results with ORB-SLAM3’s stereo-inertial setup, but I had a good experience with both OpenVINS and RTAB-Map. One key piece of advice: make sure your IMU and cameras are fully synchronized before using any of these packages. It’s important to log and visualize the timestamps, for each image frame, you should have around 5 to 10 IMU samples. This synchronization is very important for stable and accurate visual-inertial odometry.   Best regards, Mahmoud

With these matrices we can find for each point of one image its possible correspondences in the other image, along the epipolar line. To find the Fundamental (F) and Essential (E) matrices, you will need a set of characteristic points on the images, as well as the correspondences between them. OpenCV gives you functions for finding characteristic points of the SIFT or SURF type. It also gives functions for matching descriptors. We assume that the inertial frame of reference is identical to the camera frame at the left position. Then we calculate the rotation matrix R and the translation vector T for the second position. To decompose E and recover the camera pose at the second position, you can use the function recoverPose(E, K, matches). 5.
